newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW-CBOE chief sees light pressure from OTC.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-CBOE chief sees light pressure from OTC.

text.p: The fear of losing options order flow to over-the-counter (OTC) options, which are largely unregulated, is not a big concern of the Chicago Board Options Exchange (CBOE), exchange chairman and chief executive officer William Brodsky said.
"I don't look at it as a big concern," he said in an interview at an options industry conference here.

"I look at it as something to keep an eye on on one hand but also as an opportunity," he said. "Any time the firms do these OTC products, there's a natural demand and need to hedge off their own risk."
He said his goal is to make the CBOE a "hospitable" place for firms to lay off their risk from custom OTC options if they do not use the CBOE as their primary execution center.
"What you have here is the benefit of the liquidity and the clearing backup system," he said. "So there are reasons why you would do it at the exchange."
Separately, Brodsky said any further options exchange consolidation would be diffucult now that there are only four U.S. exchanges.
Last Monday, the CBOE opened a new trading floor integrating the options business it bought from the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE), which exited the options business.
Listed options are now traded on the CBOE, the American Stock Exchange, the Philadelphia Stock Exchange and the Pacific Exchange.
"I think any other consolidation at this point would be much harder," he said. "You're dealing with such bigger critical masses."
"These things get talked about a lot, but getting them done is very hard," he said.
He said he was not aware of any discussions about any other exchange mergers or buyouts. The CBOE paid $5 million for the NYSE's options business.
